title: Welcome and Table of Contents
summary: What SS1 Further Mathematics First Term is about, how to use the notes, and a map of every unit.

p: Further Mathematics goes deeper than ordinary Mathematics. It trains you to reason carefully and to solve problems in many steps, and it prepares you for science, engineering, economics, computing and university mathematics. In First Term you will study sets, indices and logarithms, surds, inequalities, binary operations, functions, and sequences and series.

Work with a pencil and a notebook. Copy every worked example and cover the solution, then try it yourself. At the end of each unit are practice questions. They do not count towards a mark; they help you check that you understood. Answer them all correctly to complete the unit.

title: Sets (1): Meaning, Notation, Types, Subsets and Power Sets
summary: What a set is, how to write sets, the types of set, the universal set, subsets and the power set, with worked examples.

p: A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects, called elements or members. 'Well-defined' means we can say for certain whether something belongs to the set or not. 'Distinct' means no repetition.

Well-defined: A = {the months of the year}. Not well-defined: B = {beautiful flowers}, because 'beautiful' is a matter of opinion. Sets are everywhere: the students in a class, the natural numbers, the letters of the alphabet.
Roster (listing) method: write the elements inside curly brackets. A = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10}.

Set-builder notation: describe the property. A = {x : x is an even number, 0 < x ≤ 10}. Read: 'A is the set of all x such that x is an even number from 1 to 10'. (The vertical bar | is often used instead of the colon.)

head: Symbol
Meaning

rows: is a subset of (may be equal)

p: Null (empty) set ∅: has no elements, such as the set of humans who can fly unaided. Singleton set: has exactly one element. Finite set: the elements can be counted to an end, such as {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}. Infinite set: the elements never end, such as {1, 2, 3, ...}. Equal sets: exactly the same elements, {1, 2, 3} = {3, 1, 2} (order does not matter). Equivalent sets: the same number of elements, such as {a, b, c} and {1, 2, 3}.
The universal set U is the set of all objects being discussed. It depends on the problem. If U = {1, 2, ..., 10} and A = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10}, then A is a subset of U.

If every element of A is also in B, then A is a subset of B, written A ⊆ B. A proper subset is a subset that is not equal to the whole set. Every set is a subset of itself, and the empty set is a subset of every set. Example: A = {1, 2}, B = {1, 2, 3, 4}, so A ⊂ B. (The source notes call ∅ an 'improper' subset. In fact, the only improper subset of A is A itself; ∅ is a proper subset of any non-empty set.)
The power set P(A) is the set of all subsets of A. If A has n elements, it has 2ⁿ subsets, so n(P(A)) = 2ⁿ, and it has 2ⁿ − 1 proper subsets.
Example: A = {a, b}. Subsets: ∅, {a}, {b}, {a, b}. So P(A) = {∅, {a}, {b}, {a, b}} and n(P(A)) = 4.
Example 1. V = {a, e, i, o, u}. (a) Set-builder: V = {x : x is a vowel in the English alphabet}. (b) Finite. (c) n(V) = 5. (d) a ∈ V is true. (e) b ∉ V.
Example 2. C = {red, green}. Subsets: ∅, {red}, {green}, {red, green}; n(P(C)) = 4.
Example 3. A set X has 63 proper subsets. How many elements? 2ⁿ − 1 = 63, so 2ⁿ = 64 and n = 6.
Example 4. List the elements of P = {x : x is prime and 10 < x < 25}. P = {11, 13, 17, 19, 23}.

summary: Union, intersection, complement and difference of sets, the inclusion-exclusion rule, and how to solve two-set problems with a Venn diagram.

p: Study the table. Suppose U = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {3, 4, 5}.

p: A Venn diagram (invented by John Venn about 1880) shows sets as pictures. The rectangle is the universal set U. Circles are subsets. Where circles overlap we have the intersection. To make a Venn diagram of two sets A and B, draw two overlapping circles inside a rectangle. There are four regions: A only, A ∩ B, B only and outside both circles.
For two sets: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B). We subtract the intersection because it was counted twice.
Also: n(A only) = n(A) − n(A ∩ B), and n(outside) = n(U) − n(A ∪ B).
In a class of 35 students, 20 offer Physics (P), 17 offer History (H) and 5 offer neither. Find (a) how many offer both, (b) how many offer History only.

n(P ∪ H) = 35 − 5 = 30. Using n(P ∪ H) = n(P) + n(H) − n(P ∩ H): 30 = 20 + 17 − n(P ∩ H), so n(P ∩ H) = 7. (a) Both = 7. (b) History only = 17 − 7 = 10. Physics only = 20 − 7 = 13. Check: 13 + 7 + 10 + 5 = 35.

If n(A \ B) = 15, n(B \ A) = 10 and n(A ∩ B) = 5, then n(A ∪ B) = 15 + 10 + 5 = 30. If 15 play football and 12 play basketball, and 5 play both, and every student plays at least one, the class has 15 + 12 − 5 = 22 students.

title: Sets (3): Three-Set Problems and De Morgan's Laws
summary: The inclusion-exclusion rule for three sets, filling a three-circle Venn diagram from the middle outward, and De Morgan's laws.

p: A three-set Venn diagram has eight regions: A ∩ B ∩ C in the centre; three regions where exactly two sets overlap; three regions of 'only' one set; and the region outside all the circles.

img.alt: A three-circle Venn diagram of sets F, C and P with all eight region values filled in: F only 20, C only 12, P only 20, F and C only 8, F and P only 5, C and P only 3, all three 7, none 25
img.cap: The three-set Venn diagram for the worked example.

p: n(A ∪ B ∪ C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) − n(A ∩ B) − n(A ∩ C) − n(B ∩ C) + n(A ∩ B ∩ C).
Of 100 people, 40 belong to club F, 30 to club C and 35 to club P. The overlaps: n(F ∩ C) = 15, n(F ∩ P) = 12, n(C ∩ P) = 10 and n(F ∩ C ∩ P) = 7.

Always start from the middle. Region F ∩ C ∩ P = 7. F ∩ C only = 15 − 7 = 8. F ∩ P only = 12 − 7 = 5. C ∩ P only = 10 − 7 = 3. F only = 40 − (8 + 5 + 7) = 20. C only = 30 − (8 + 3 + 7) = 12. P only = 35 − (5 + 3 + 7) = 20. Total inside the circles = 20 + 12 + 20 + 8 + 5 + 3 + 7 = 75. So 100 − 75 = 25 are in none.

For any sets A and B: (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ and (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′. In words: 'the complement of the union is the intersection of the complements', and 'the complement of the intersection is the union of the complements'.

Check with U = {a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h}, X = {a, b, d, e} and Y = {b, e, f, g}. X ∪ Y = {a, b, d, e, f, g}, so (X ∪ Y)′ = {c, h}. X′ = {c, f, g, h} and Y′ = {a, c, d, h}, so X′ ∩ Y′ = {c, h}. They agree. Also X′ ∩ Y = {f, g}.

A survey of 60 fans: 28 watch football, 22 basketball, 25 cricket; 10 watch football and basketball, 8 watch football and cricket, 7 watch basketball and cricket; 3 watch all three. Centre = 3. F ∩ B only = 7; F ∩ C only = 5; B ∩ C only = 4. F only = 28 − (7 + 5 + 3) = 13. B only = 22 − (7 + 4 + 3) = 8. C only = 25 − (5 + 4 + 3) = 13. Exactly two sports: 7 + 5 + 4 = 16. Inside the circles: 13 + 8 + 13 + 7 + 5 + 4 + 3 = 53, so 60 − 53 = 7 watch none.

activity: State De Morgan's laws. Verify (X ∩ Y)′ = X′ ∪ Y′ for the sets X and Y above. (X ∩ Y = {b, e}; its complement is {a, c, d, f, g, h}. X′ ∪ Y′ = {c, f, g, h} ∪ {a, c, d, h} = {a, c, d, f, g, h}.)

title: Indices
summary: The meaning of an index (power) and the laws of indices, zero, negative and fractional indices, worked examples and indicial equations.

p: Indices (powers) show repeated multiplication. a⁵ = a × a × a × a × a. Here a is the base and 5 is the index (exponent), the number of times the base is multiplied by itself. Example: 2⁵ = 32.
For any positive base a and any numbers m and n:
Example 1. Simplify (16/81)^(−3/4). A negative index inverts the fraction: (81/16)^(3/4). Now the fourth root of 81 is 3 and of 16 is 2, so we get (3/2)³ = 27/8.
Example 2. Evaluate 8^(2/3) × 2⁻². 8^(2/3) = (∛8)² = 4. 2⁻² = 1/4. The product is 1.
An indicial equation has the unknown in the index. Method: write both sides with the same base, then equate the indices.
Example 4. Solve 3^(x) = 81. 81 = 3⁴ so x = 4. Example 5. Solve (1/4)^x = 32. Write both as powers of 2: (2⁻²)^x = 2⁵, so −2x = 5 and x = −5/2.

Example 6 (quadratic form). Solve 4^x − 6(2^x) + 8 = 0. Let y = 2^x. Then 4^x = (2²)^x = (2^x)² = y². So y² − 6y + 8 = 0, which factorises as (y − 2)(y − 4) = 0, so y = 2 or y = 4. Then 2^x = 2 gives x = 1, and 2^x = 4 gives x = 2. Answer: x = 1 or x = 2.
Example 7. Solve 5^(2k) + 2(5^k) − 3 = 0. Let y = 5^k: y² + 2y − 3 = 0, (y + 3)(y − 1) = 0. y = −3 is impossible (5^k is always positive). So 5^k = 1 and k = 0.

The graph of y = 2^x rises faster and faster as x increases (exponential growth). The graph of y = (1/2)^x falls towards zero (exponential decay). Both pass through (0, 1) because any number to the power 0 is 1.

img.alt: Graphs of y = 2 to the power x rising steeply and y = one half to the power x falling, both passing through the point (0, 1)

title: Logarithms
summary: The meaning of a logarithm, the laws of logarithms, change of base, and solving logarithmic equations.

p: Logarithms do the opposite of indices. If aˣ = N, then log_a N = x, read 'the logarithm of N to base a equals x'. It tells us the power to which the base must be raised to give N.

Examples: 10³ = 1000, so log₁₀ 1000 = 3. 2⁵ = 32, so log₂ 32 = 5. Because log₁₀ 100 = 2, we say 'the log of 100 to base 10 is 2'. Indices and logarithms are two ways of writing the same fact: aˣ = N ⇔ log_a N = x.
Study the table. M and N must be positive.
log_a b = log_c b ÷ log_c a (usually c = 10 or e). A useful corollary: log_a b = 1 ÷ log_b a.
Example. Given log₃ 2 = 0.631, find log₂ 9. log₂ 9 = log₃ 9 ÷ log₃ 2 = 2 ÷ 0.631 = 3.17.
Example 1. Evaluate log₂ 8 + log₃ 9 − log₅ 1. = 3 + 2 − 0 = 5.
Example 2. Express ½ log 25 − 2 log 3 + log 18 as a single logarithm. ½ log 25 = log 5. 2 log 3 = log 9. So log 5 − log 9 + log 18 = log (5 × 18 ÷ 9) = log 10 = 1 (to base 10).
Example 3. Given log₁₀ 2 = 0.3010, find log₁₀ 32. 32 = 2⁵, so log 32 = 5 × 0.3010 = 1.505.

Example 4 (equation). Solve log₂ x + log₂ (x − 7) = 3. Combine: log₂ [x(x − 7)] = 3, so x(x − 7) = 2³ = 8. Then x² − 7x − 8 = 0, (x − 8)(x + 1) = 0. x = 8 or x = −1. We reject −1 because log of a negative number does not exist. Answer: x = 8.
Example 5. Solve log₃ p − log₃ (p − 6) = 2. log₃ [p/(p − 6)] = 2, so p/(p − 6) = 9, p = 9p − 54, 8p = 54, p = 6.75.
Example 6. Solve log₄(x + 1) + log₄(x − 1) = log₄ 8. (x + 1)(x − 1) = 8, x² = 9, x = 3 (reject −3).

title: Surds
summary: What surds are, the rules for simplifying, adding and multiplying them, and how to rationalise a denominator.

p: A surd is an irrational root that cannot be simplified to remove the root sign, such as √2, √3, √5 and ∛5. √4 = 2 and √9 = 3 are not surds, because they are rational numbers. A simple surd is one term, like √7. A compound surd joins a surd to another term, like 2 + √3 or 5 − 2√2.
Study the table.
To rationalise means to remove the surd from the denominator.
Monomial denominator: multiply top and bottom by the surd. 6/√3 = (6 × √3)/(√3 × √3) = 6√3/3 = 2√3.
Binomial denominator: multiply top and bottom by the conjugate. The conjugate of a + √b is a − √b (change the sign in the middle). This uses (a + √b)(a − √b) = a² − b, which has no surd.
Example 2. Rationalise 1/(2 + √3). Multiply by (2 − √3): (2 − √3)/(4 − 3) = 2 − √3.

title: Linear Inequalities in One Variable
summary: Inequality symbols, solving linear inequalities, the golden rule for negative numbers, and showing answers on a number line.

p: An inequality shows that one side is bigger or smaller than the other. Symbols: > (greater than), < (less than), ≥ (greater than or equal to), ≤ (less than or equal to). A linear inequality has a variable only to the first power, such as 2x + 5 > 9 or 3x − 4 ≤ 8.
Solve a linear inequality like an equation, but when you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number, reverse the inequality sign.
Why: 6 > 4 is true. Multiply by −2: −12 and −8. −12 > −8 is false; the true statement is −12 < −8.
Open circle ○ for < or > (the end point is not included). Closed circle ● for ≤ or ≥ (the end point is included). An arrow shows the direction of all the solutions.
x > 2: open circle at 2, arrow to the right. x ≤ −3: closed circle at −3, arrow to the left. 2 ≤ x < 6: closed circle at 2, open circle at 6, a line between.
Example 1. Solve 5 − 2x ≥ 11. −2x ≥ 6. Divide by −2 and reverse the sign: x ≤ −3. Closed circle at −3, arrow left.
Example 2. Solve 3x − 5 < 4x + 2. −5 − 2 < 4x − 3x, so −7 < x, or x > −7. Open circle at −7, arrow right.
Example 3 (double inequality). Solve −1 ≤ 2x − 5 < 7. Add 5: 4 ≤ 2x < 12. Divide by 2: 2 ≤ x < 6.
Example 4. Solve and represent x/2 − 5 > −8. x/2 > −3, so x > −6.
Example 5. Solve 7 − 4x ≤ 1. −4x ≤ −6, so x ≥ 3/2.
Example 6. Solve −5 ≤ 3x + 1 ≤ 10. −6 ≤ 3x ≤ 9, so −2 ≤ x ≤ 3.
Example 8. Find the range of x for 3x − 2 > 7 and x − 1 < 5. First: x > 3. Second: x < 6. So 3 < x < 6.
